Completeness of (M,d) implies that, for every sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets with F_{n+1}\subset F_n and the diameter of F_n tending to 0, one can construct a Cauchy sequence from those sets.
Can one build that Cauchy sequence explicitly?
If points x_n are selected from the sets F_n, then for every \epsilon>0 there is N with the diameter of F_N < \epsilon, so d(x_m,x_n)<\epsilon whenever m,n\ge N, and completeness gives a limit x in M for (x_n).
Does that limit x lie in every F_n?
The limit x lies in each F_n, because x_k \in F_n for all k \ge n and F_n is closed, so x \in \bigcap_n F_n.
How does the reverse implication force completeness?
For any Cauchy sequence (y_n), there are strictly increasing N_n such that the diameter of \{y_k \mid k \ge N_n\} < 1/n.
The sets G_n defined as the closures of the tails \{y_k \mid k \ge N_n\} are nonempty and closed, satisfy G_{n+1}\subset G_n, and have diameter at most 1/n, so their diameters tend to 0.
By the assumed intersection property, \bigcap_n G_n is nonempty, and if x \in \bigcap_n G_n, then d(x,y_m) \le 1/n for all m \ge N_n, so (y_n) converges to x and M is complete.
